title: The poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3)
hook: blessed are the poor in spirit: the empty-handed have room for the kingdom

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus went up the mountain and sat down, and your line was sit down, listen. Did you let someone finish before you spoke? Day two hundred thirty-three.

Hashtag blessed. You've seen it under photos of a new car, a beach, a baby, a promotion. Blessed means things are going well. So imagine sitting on that hillside. The crowd is full of fishermen, farmers, the sick and the poor. Jesus has just sat down, and everyone leans in for the first words of his great sermon. And he opens with a list of people who are blessed. Only the list doesn't include anyone with a new car. It starts with the people who have nothing.
screen: `HASHTAG BLESSED.` → `THE FIRST WORDS OF THE SERMON.` → `IT STARTS WITH THE EMPTY-HANDED.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." This is the first of the Beatitudes, from the Latin beatus, blessed. Matthew's Greek word is makarios. It meant happy, fortunate, well off, the word Greeks used for the gods and the rich. And its Hebrew cousin opens the book of Psalms: blessed is the man. So when Jesus says makarios, it's partly a congratulation. Lucky you. You're in a good place. Then look who he congratulates. The Greek word for poor here doesn't mean a little short this month. It's the word for a beggar, someone with empty hands. Luke's version just says blessed be ye poor. Matthew adds in spirit, and Christians have read that in more than one way. Some hear the humble: people who know they can't earn their way to God. Others hear those who are poor and have no pride left to hold on to. Many read both together. Either way, it's the opposite of self-sufficient. And the promise isn't someday. It's theirs is the kingdom of heaven, present tense. Here's the picture that helps. You can't receive a gift with your hands full. If you're clutching your phone, your coffee and your bags, someone has to wait while you put something down. The poor in spirit already have their hands open. That's why this beatitude comes first. Everything else in the sermon is a gift, and it's the empty hands that can take it.
screen: `MAKARIOS: BLESSED, FORTUNATE.` · `POOR: A BEGGAR'S EMPTY HANDS.` · `IN SPIRIT: TWO READINGS.` · `THEIRS IS THE KINGDOM, NOW.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE POOR IN SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: admit one need. Settle, and breathe. Rest your hands on your knees, palms open, facing up. Now think of one thing you can't do on your own right now. Help you need, and haven't asked for. Something you can't fix. Just name it, quietly, to yourself. No shame in it. Let your open hands say what's true: I don't have everything. If you pray, you can bring that need to God with your hands open. The bell holds the time.
Blessed. Makarios in Greek: fortunate, well off, congratulations. And Jesus says it first to the poor in spirit.
Your line: empty hands can receive. Today, ask one person for help with something real, and let yourself receive it without paying it back right away. Day two hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Many Christians know the Beatitudes by heart; Orthodox churches sing them in the Divine Liturgy most Sundays, and they're read in many churches on All Saints' Day.

myth: the Greek for blessed meant fortunate or well off
makarios: happy, fortunate, a word used of the gods and the rich.
Luke's version also says poor in spirit
Luke says blessed be ye poor. Matthew adds in spirit.
the promise of the first beatitude is only for the future
theirs is the kingdom of heaven: present tense.

fork.setup: a teacher sits down on a hillside and begins his most famous sermon. who does he call blessed first?
fork.reveal: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." it starts with the empty-handed.

original.note: Greek: blessed, fortunate ones. the first word of each beatitude in Matthew 5.

trapdoor: what you thought: blessed means things are going well.
what it means: Jesus congratulates the empty-handed: theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
what a scholar hears: makarios echoes the Hebrew ashrei of Psalm 1, and the word for poor, ptochos, means a beggar.

sources.quoted: Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

notes: makarios used of the gods and the fortunate in classical Greek: standard lexicon claim; confirm phrasing 'the gods and the rich'.
ptochos (beggar, destitute) vs penes (working poor): standard distinction; confirm.
Readings of 'in spirit' are presented as held by different Christians without ranking.
Orthodox Divine Liturgy: the Beatitudes are sung as the third antiphon on many Sundays (typika); confirm phrasing 'most Sundays'.
